nameStory: Hoary alyssum gets its name from its distinctly fuzzy, grayish-white appearance - 'hoary' means grayish-white or covered with fine white hairs, just like this plant's leaves and stems. The word 'alyssum' comes from the Greek words meaning 'without madness,' as ancient Greeks believed plants in this group could cure rabies and calm anger.
description: Hoary alyssum is a knee-high flowering plant that looks like it's been dusted with gray powder. This member of the mustard family produces clusters of tiny white flowers above fuzzy, gray-green leaves that feel soft and velvety to the touch. It's a biennial herb, meaning it takes two years to complete its life cycle, and can grow 1-3 feet tall with a branched, somewhat sprawling growth habit.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Gray-green leaves covered in fine, soft hairs that give them a distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture - run your finger along one and you'll immediately feel the difference from smooth-leaved plants

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in dense, rounded clusters at the branch tips - each petal is deeply notched, giving it a heart-shaped appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Branched stems that spread outward and upward, creating a somewhat bushy appearance that's wider at the top than at the base

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, oval seed pods that are flattened and hairy, containing tiny seeds that give the plant a slightly rattling sound when mature pods are shaken

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Covered in the same fine, grayish hairs as the leaves, making the entire plant appear softly fuzzy and giving it an overall silvery-gray cast

habitat: Look for hoary alyssum along roadsides, in disturbed soils, abandoned fields, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained, often sandy or gravelly soils and tolerates drought well. You'll commonly spot it in areas where the soil has been disturbed by human activity, such as construction sites, parking lot edges, and railroad rights-of-way.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as fuzzy rosettes of gray-green leaves close to the ground, easily recognizable by their distinctly velvety texture.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with clusters of small white flowers covering the branched stems, making the plant quite showy and easy to spot from a distance.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed pods develop, turning brown and papery while still maintaining the plant's characteristic fuzzy appearance.
seasonality.winter: Annual stems die back, but in milder areas some basal rosettes may persist through winter, appearing as small patches of gray-fuzzy leaves.

funFact: Despite being called 'alyssum,' this plant isn't actually related to the popular garden alyssum - it's a completely different genus that just happens to share a common name, showing how tricky plant names can be!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with sweet alyssum (Lobularia maritima), the popular garden flower, but hoary alyssum is much taller, has distinctly fuzzy gray leaves (sweet alyssum's are smooth and green), and grows wild rather than in neat garden borders. Remember: if it's fuzzy and gray, it's hoary alyssum.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of those confusing plant names where 'alyssum' refers to two completely unrelated plants - the sweet alyssum commonly grown in gardens belongs to genus Lobularia, while hoary alyssum is in genus Berteroa. Both are in the mustard family, but they're as different as distant cousins.
compareHints: Hoary alyssum is the only member of genus Berteroa found in New England, making it unique in this regard. Within the mustard family, it's most similar to other small white-flowered species like field pennycress or shepherd's purse, but neither of those has the distinctive fuzzy, gray-green foliage that makes hoary alyssum instantly recognizable.
